RECAP: Session 13 : IAM Fundamentals

Agenda for Today's Session
1. Roles & Temporary Credentials: Assuming a role; session tokens; temporary vs long-lived credentials
2. Principle of Least Privilege: Scoping actions & resources; wildcards & their risks; permission boundaries; iterative tightening
3. Federation & Single Sign-On: Identity providers; SAML & OIDC; multi-factor authentication (MFA)

slides.title: Temporary Identity Map
slides.lead: IAM users hold permissions and credentials permanently. A role is a different identity type, assumed only for the duration a task needs, then given up

points.text: Assuming a role: how a caller temporarily becomes that identity
Temporary credential set: access key, secret key, session token
Expiry window: credentials stop working after a fixed duration
Trust policy: controls who is allowed to assume the role

slides.notes: Position roles as the identity type used instead of permanent keys, distinct from users and groups. Point out that a role has no login of its own. Exam hook: roles are the standard answer to 'how do I avoid storing permanent keys'.

slides.title: Borrowed Permissions
slides.lead: A role is a set of permissions that any trusted caller can borrow for a while, rather than an identity someone logs into directly. Formally, it is an IAM identity with a permission policy and a trust policy, but no password or permanent keys

points.text: Trust policy names which account, service or user may assume it
Permission policy defines what the role can do once assumed
Usable by people, applications, or other AWS services alike
Exists independently of any single employee or application

slides.notes: Say the gate-pass line slowly, it is the anchor for the whole section. Point to the trust policy as the gatekeeper, visible on a role's Trust relationships tab in the IAM console. Interviewers often ask why roles beat embedding keys: this slide is the answer.

slides.label: Analogy: library card
slides.title: Borrowed Permissions
slides.notes:
TR analogy: Borrowing a library book using a library card. You can use the book for a limited period and must return it afterward, just as a role provides temporary permissions that expire after the session.

Say the gate-pass line slowly, it is the anchor for the whole section. Point to the trust policy as the gatekeeper, visible on a role's Trust relationships tab in the IAM console. Interviewers often ask why roles beat embedding keys: this slide is the answer.

slides.title: AssumeRole Flow
slides.lead: Assuming a role is a request, not a login: a caller already holding some identity asks AWS Security Token Service (STS) to hand over the role's permissions for a limited time

points.text: Caller invokes `sts:AssumeRole`, naming the target role's ARN
STS checks the role's trust policy allows that caller
Caller also needs its own permission to call AssumeRole

slides.notes: Stress that trusting an account does not auto-grant every identity in it the right to assume; the caller still needs AssumeRole permission. This is exactly what a role's Trust relationships tab in the IAM console shows. Exam hook: trust policy versus permission policy is a frequent interview trap.

slides.title: AssumeRole Flow

points.text: The caller uses the temporary credentials to make requests with the assumed role's permissions
STS returns a fresh, time-limited credential set for the role

slides.notes: Stress that trusting an account does not auto-grant every identity in it the right to assume; the caller still needs AssumeRole permission. This is exactly what a role's Trust relationships tab in the IAM console shows. Exam hook: trust policy versus permission policy is a frequent interview trap.

slides.title: Token And Expiry
slides.lead: A successful assume-role call returns three values together, not just a key pair, because the session token is what marks the credentials as temporary rather than permanent

points.text: Access key ID and secret access key: sign each request's authentication
Session token: must accompany every call, proves temporary origin

slides.notes: Clarify the session token is not optional: omitting it makes the request fail even with a valid key pair. Likely exam question: name the three parts of a temporary credential set.

slides.title: Token And Expiry

points.text: Role maximum session duration: configurable from 1 to 12 hours
The requested session duration cannot exceed this limit
After expiry, the caller must assume the role again for new credentials

slides.notes: Point out the duration setting is configured on the role itself.

slides.title: Credential Comparison
slides.lead: Long-lived access keys, created for a user, stay valid until someone deletes them; temporary credentials from a role expire on their own, which changes the risk a leaked credential carries
slides.notes: Use the table to make the exposure-window argument concrete rather than abstract. Point at the leak-exposure row as the practical reason cloud security teams push roles over keys. This comparison is a near-guaranteed interview question.

slides.title: Four Tightening Levers
slides.lead: A policy written to get a job done quickly often grants far more than the job needs; least privilege is the discipline of trimming that grant down to exactly what is required

points.text: Scoping: naming the exact actions and resources allowed
Wildcards: the asterisk symbol and the risk it hides
Permission boundaries: a hard ceiling on an identity's access
Iterative tightening: narrowing a grant as real usage is observed

slides.notes: Frame this as the discipline behind every policy written in the IAM console. State the four levers by name before going into each one. Flag that interviewers often ask how to tighten an over-permissioned role: these four levers are the answer.

slides.title: Narrow The Grant
slides.lead: The Action and Resource fields of a policy statement are where scope is actually narrowed, turning a broad grant into one that matches only the task at hand

points.text: Action field names one API call, not an entire service
Resource field names one ARN, not every resource
Separate statements per service keep each grant narrow
Narrower scope shrinks the blast radius of a leaked credential

slides.notes: Point out that Action and Resource fields are used deliberately here to narrow access, not merely to describe it. Ask: why scope Resource even when Action is already specific? Mention the IAM policy editor as where this scoping is actually written.

slides.title: The Asterisk Danger
slides.lead: A wildcard, written as the asterisk (*), tells AWS to match every possible value in a field instead of one. Placed in Action or Resource, it grants far more access than a single task needs

points.text: Action as asterisk can grant every AWS API action
Resource as asterisk matches every object, not a chosen ARN
Action and Resource both as asterisk grant full control of the whole AWS account
A compromised credential then exposes every resource the wildcard covers

slides.notes: Say plainly that the asterisk is convenient but dangerous precisely because it never expires or narrows on its own. Point to the circled asterisks in the snippet while explaining the blast radius. A favourite interview probe: what is wrong with Resource colon asterisk on an S3 policy?

slides.label: Analogy: building-wide access card
slides.title: The Asterisk Danger
slides.notes:
TR analogy: A building-wide access card that opens every room when only one room's access was needed: just as a wildcard can grant access far beyond what a task requires.

Say plainly that the asterisk is convenient but dangerous precisely because it never expires or narrows on its own. Point to the circled asterisks in the snippet while explaining the blast radius. A favourite interview probe: what is wrong with Resource colon asterisk on an S3 policy?

slides.title: A Hard Ceiling
slides.lead: A permission boundary sets a hard ceiling on what an identity's own policies can ever grant, however generously those policies are written. It is itself a managed policy, evaluated alongside the identity policy

points.text: Boundary itself grants no permissions on its own
Boundary only limits permissions granted elsewhere
Often applied so a team lead cannot escalate their own role
Attached per user or role, not inside a policy document

slides.notes: Stress that a boundary cannot add access, only subtract from what the identity policy already allows. Point to the overlap region in the diagram as the effective permission. This distinction between granting and capping is a common interview trap.

slides.label: Analogy: floor access card
slides.title: A Hard Ceiling
slides.notes:
TR analogy: A building access card allows an employee to enter only approved floors, even if their department's rules allow access to more floors: just as a permission boundary limits the maximum permissions an identity can receive.

Stress that a boundary cannot add access, only subtract from what the identity policy already allows. Point to the overlap region in the diagram as the effective permission. This distinction between granting and capping is a common interview trap.

slides.title: Narrowing A Grant
slides.lead: Iterative tightening starts an identity wide enough to work, then narrows the policy in passes as real usage confirms what it actually calls

cells: IAM Access Analyzer reviews 30 days of CloudTrail activity: only `s3:GetObject` and `s3:PutObject` used
Confirms only two calls are invoked
Matches only the calls actually seen

slides.notes: Walk the table pass by pass, pointing out that the second pass uses real usage evidence, not guesswork, to decide the narrower statement. Name IAM Access Analyzer as the console feature that supplies this evidence. Interview angle: this four-pass pattern is the standard answer to right-sizing an IAM policy over time.

slides.title: Narrowing A Grant
slides.lead: Each pass trades early convenience for a smaller blast radius, ending with a policy that matches exactly what the workload does

Name IAM Access Analyzer as the console feature that supplies this evidence. Interview angle: this four-pass pattern is the standard answer to right-sizing an IAM policy over time.

slides.title: Identity Providers
slides.lead: A separate password per cloud application does not scale past a handful of staff. Federation lets an external identity provider (IdP) verify an employee once, and the cloud trusts that proof instead of checking a password itself

points.text: Login request redirects from AWS to the company IdP
AWS trusts the signed proof, no password stored on its side
Trust is pre-configured between AWS and the IdP beforehand
One IdP can serve AWS, other clouds and on-premise apps

slides.notes: Explain the redirect as the core mechanism, not a login form on AWS itself. Say plainly: AWS never sees the password, only the IdP's signed proof. Interview hook: ask what problem federation solves versus one IAM user per employee.

slides.label: Analogy: company ID card at branch offices
slides.title: Identity Providers
slides.notes:
TR analogy: A company ID card issued by the head office is accepted at every branch office without a fresh check: just as a federated identity, once verified by the identity provider, is trusted across every connected cloud application.

Explain the redirect as the core mechanism, not a login form on AWS itself. Say plainly: AWS never sees the password, only the IdP's signed proof. Interview hook: ask what problem federation solves versus one IAM user per employee.

slides.title: Side By Side
slides.lead: SAML and OIDC are the two standards that actually carry the IdP's signed proof to AWS; MFA and SSO describe what happens around that proof, before and after it is issued

cells: A service that verifies a user's identity
A standard used to exchange authentication information
A standard used for identity verification and authentication
Requires an additional verification step during login
Allows access to multiple applications with one login

slides.notes: Point out SAML is XML-based and older, OIDC is token-based and built on OAuth 2.0: both do the same job of carrying proof. Mention Microsoft Entra ID as a real IdP that speaks either standard to AWS. Exam hook: SAML versus OIDC is a frequent interview comparison.

slides.title: SSO In Practice
slides.lead: A policy condition can require that the current session was authenticated with multi-factor authentication (MFA), checked at request time rather than only at sign-in

points.text: Condition key `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent` is true only for sessions started with MFA
Typically guards destructive actions like delete or terminate
IAM Identity Center provides single sign-on (SSO) across many accounts
Federated users get MFA from the IdP or IAM Identity Center

slides.notes: Point to the Condition block and stress that MFA presence is checked at request time, not at login time. Say plainly: a stolen access key without MFA still gets denied on the protected action. Interview hook: ask how someone would force MFA on only destructive actions rather than all of IAM.

slides.title: Instances To Agents
slides.lead: Instances and applications act on AWS without a human typing credentials. Each needs its own identity: an instance role, a workload role, or a certificate-based identity for external systems

points.text: Instance identity: role attached to an EC2 instance via a profile
Workload identity: role attached to a Lambda function or ECS task
Anti-pattern: long-lived access keys embedded inside application code
Scale challenge: many services each needing a distinct, revocable identity

slides.notes: Frame this as the non-human counterpart to a user or role held by a person. Point to the four landscape bullets as the map for this section. Exam hook: interviewers ask why a key in code is worse than a role.

slides.title: Role On The Machine
slides.lead: An instance profile is a container that attaches an IAM role to a running EC2 instance, so the instance itself becomes the identity making calls. Lambda and ECS carry the same idea through an execution role or task role

points.text: Changing the attached role takes effect without redeploying code
Lambda execution role: permissions the function code runs under
ECS task role: scoped per task definition, not per cluster

slides.notes: Explain the instance profile as the wrapper that lets an EC2 instance hold a role. Contrast it with assigning a role directly to a person. Exam hook: an interviewer may ask what an instance profile actually contains.

slides.label: Analogy: hotel room housekeeping card
slides.title: Role On The Machine
slides.notes:
TR analogy: A hotel gives a room its own access card for housekeeping services, regardless of which staff member performs the work: just as an instance role gives the EC2 instance its own identity to access AWS services.

Explain the instance profile as the wrapper that lets an EC2 instance hold a role. Contrast it with assigning a role directly to a person. Exam hook: an interviewer may ask what an instance profile actually contains.

slides.title: Automatic And Local
slides.lead: Once a role is attached, the instance or function retrieves temporary credentials automatically, with no key typed in or stored anywhere

points.text: Instance metadata service hands out short-lived credentials locally
Credentials refresh automatically well before they expire
Lambda injects temporary credentials into the execution environment automatically
No long-lived keys needed in code or config files

slides.notes: Stress that rotation is automatic and invisible to the application code. Point to the metadata-service arrow as where credentials originate locally. Exam hook: why rotation removes the need for manual key management.

slides.title: Key Versus Role
slides.lead: Hardcoding a long-lived access key into source code ties that credential to wherever the code travels (repositories, logs, container images) long past the instance's own lifetime

cells.text: Git history, build logs, container images
Retrieved at runtime from the platform
Edit the code or config and redeploy
No code change; SDK retrieves refreshed credentials
High: may be exposed in code or files
Lower: avoids embedding long-lived keys in code or configuration files
Detach the role; access ends when current credentials expire

slides.notes: Use the table to make the trade-off concrete rather than abstract. Point at the revocation row as the clearest practical difference. Exam hook: this comparison is a common interview question on IAM best practice.

slides.title: Governing Many Machines
slides.lead: Cloud environments run far more machine identities than human ones, so the same least-privilege discipline from earlier must apply to every service, container and external system calling AWS

points.text: Each microservice gets its own scoped role, not a shared one
IAM Roles Anywhere issues temporary credentials to on-premises servers
Cross-account roles let one service assume identity in another account
Central governance tracks and revokes many non-human identities

slides.notes: Close by connecting the single-instance mechanism to the organisation-wide governance problem. Point to IAM Roles Anywhere as the bridge for non-AWS machines. Exam hook: interviewers ask how identity scales once a company runs hundreds of services.

slides.title: Scoped Short Lived
slides.lead: An AI agent, software that plans and carries out actions on its own, still needs an identity before calling any cloud API, and that identity needs the same guardrails as any machine identity

points.text: Scoped: credentials cover only the actions the task needs
Short-lived: credentials expire automatically after a session window
Revocable: access can be withdrawn the moment the task ends

slides.notes: Frame this as the machine-identity principle extended to an autonomous caller. Say plainly: an agent is just another non-human identity, so the same three guarantees apply. Interview hook: ask why a long-lived key is dangerous specifically for an agent that plans its own next step.

slides.label: Analogy: delivery worker shift card
slides.title: Scoped Short Lived
slides.notes:
TR analogy: A delivery worker receives a temporary access card that opens only the assigned delivery area and expires after the shift: just as an AI agent receives limited, short-lived credentials for its assigned task.

Frame this as the machine-identity principle extended to an autonomous caller. Say plainly: an agent is just another non-human identity, so the same three guarantees apply. Interview hook: ask why a long-lived key is dangerous specifically for an agent that plans its own next step.

slides.title: When Scope Fails
slides.lead: Excessive agency happens when an agent's granted permissions exceed what its task genuinely needs, so one bad instruction can cascade into an action nobody intended

points.text: A broad role lets one misleading instruction delete production data
Wide permissions turn a flawed plan into a real action
Scoped, short-lived, revocable credentials bound the damage one step causes
Least privilege for agents mirrors least privilege for any IAM role

slides.notes: Explain that excessive agency is not a bug in the model but a permissions design failure, same as any over-broad IAM role. Point out the parallel with the broad ec2:* example discussed in the practical. Interview hook: ask how scoping, short expiry and revocability each independently limit the blast radius of one wrong agent action.

Quiz on IAM Roles & Least Privilege. Q1. How do you avoid storing permanent keys? Answer: Use a role. Q2. Name the three parts of a temporary credential set. Answer: Access key ID, secret access key and session token. Q3. Which policy decides who may assume a role, and which decides what it can do? Answer: The trust policy and the permission policy. Q4. What is wrong with Resource set to the asterisk on an S3 policy? Answer: It matches every object, not a chosen ARN. Q5. Can a permission boundary add access? Answer: No, it only limits permissions granted elsewhere. Q6. What does federation let AWS trust instead of a password? Answer: The identity provider's signed proof. Q7. Which condition key forces MFA on destructive actions? Answer: aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent. Q8. Why is a key in code worse than a role? Answer: It travels with the code and must be found and replaced everywhere; a role's credentials are retrieved at runtime and expire.

1. Roles & Temporary Credentials: Assuming a role; session tokens; temporary vs long-lived credentials
2. Principle of Least Privilege: Scoping actions & resources; wildcards & their risks; permission boundaries; iterative tightening
3. Federation & Single Sign-On: Identity providers; SAML & OIDC; multi-factor authentication (MFA)
4. Service & Machine Identity: Instance & workload identities; avoiding embedded keys; non-human identity at scale
5. Identity for AI Agents: Scoped, short-lived & revocable credentials; excessive agency as a failure mode
